(CNN) -- Ten people were killed Tuesday when a gunman rampaged through a Finnish college, police officials said. Officials say Matti Juhani Saari began firing in a classroom at the college before shooting himself. Over the course of 90 minutes, Saari fired a few shots at police, Finnish broadcaster YLE said. Jukka Forsberg, a maintenance worker at the school, told YLE that the gunman was wearing a ski mask and walked into the building with a large bag. About 150 students were on campus Kauhajoki city's School of Hospitality in southwestern Finland. Forsberg said, "I heard several dozen rounds of shots. In other words, it was an automatic pistol. I saw some female students who were wailing and moaning, and one managed to escape out the back door." Smoke billowed from a building on campus, but officials could not immediately say what caused the fire.  Watch pictures from the scene » . Tapio Varmola, who was visiting the school at the time, told CNN he was in a building about two blocks away when the shootings occurred. After the shootings, he said, he heard students shouting. Police came about 10 minutes after they were called, Varmola said. "It took two hours to get this situation ended," he said. Saari, 22, died Tuesday afternoon from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head at Tampere University Hospital, said medical director Matti Lehto. At least one other person suffered serious injuries in the shooting, he added. Police had interviewed and released Saari on Monday after he posted violent videos on YouTube, authorities said. As Saari did not directly threaten anyone in the videos, there were no grounds for further action, national police Commissioner Mikko Paatero told YLE. Authorities learned about the videos Friday but could not reach Saari until Monday, Paatero told YLE. Police also searched his home, YLE reported. Four videos of a man firing a pistol at a shooting range were posted by a "Mr. Saari" from Kauhajoki, where the college is based, according to his YouTube profile. The profile also included a video tribute to the Columbine High School shooters, Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold, at the top of the man's favorites list. The videos were posted over a three-week period this month. None was posted in the last week.  Watch more about the YouTube videos » . The account was suspended within hours of the shooting, which began about 11 a.m. local time (0800 GMT). MTV-3's Foreign Editor Risto Puolimatka told CNN that Saari was also issued with a temporary gun license last month. It was the gunman's first license, Puolimatka said. Finnish President Tarja Halonen expressed her condolences from the United Nations, where she is attending the annual General Assembly. She also commented on the YouTube videos. "We, parents and elderly people, have a little bit of feeling about the Internet," she said at an impromptu TV interview. "It's like a strange planet for us. But it's not so. It's part of our world, so we have to step in." She praised efforts by police, who she said "were already on board" by interviewing Saari. Authorities hoped that was enough to take care of any threat, but "now we see that it was not," she said. The school taught late teens and young adults, Jarkko Sipila of MTV 3 told CNN. "It's more or less like an agricultural or professional school where people teach how to make food or how to cook in big kitchen, in industrial kitchens," he said. Kauhajoki, with a population of about 15,000, is about 290km (180 miles) from the capital, Helsinki. The incident comes almost a year after another school shooting left nine people, including the gunman, dead in the Finnish town of Tuusala. Before that shooting, the gunman, 18-year-old student Pekka-Eric Auvinen, posted a video on YouTube titled "Jokela High School Massacre 11/7/2007," identifying the date and location of the attack. "All these memories are being brought back and people are asking the question, 'Why again?' " Sipila said. Finland enjoys a strong tradition of hunting and has a high proportion of gun ownership, with 2 million firearms owned in a nation of 5 million people.

The profile’s list of favorite videos was headed by a tribute to Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold, the perpetrators of the Columbine High School attack. The four shooting-range clips were uploaded during a three-week span that month, though none had been added in the preceding week.

YouTube suspended the account within hours of the college shooting, which started at approximately 11 a.m. local time, or 0800 GMT.

# BREAKING NEWS

## Gunman kills 10 at Finnish college before taking his own life

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland, September 23, 2008** — A 22-year-old student opened fire at a vocational college in western Finland on Tuesday, killing 10 people before fatally shooting himself, authorities said.

Police identified the attacker as **Matti Juhani Saari**, a culinary arts student at the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality, part of Seinäjoki University of Applied Sciences. Officials said nine students and one staff member were killed. Another woman was wounded. The gunman later died at a hospital, bringing the total death toll to 11.

Witnesses told Finnish news organizations that they heard repeated gunfire shortly after classes began. Some described seeing a man dressed in dark clothing and wearing a mask moving through the building with a firearm and a bag. Students fled through doors and windows as smoke rose from the school, where fires had been set during the attack.

Emergency crews and heavily armed police surrounded the campus, evacuating survivors and searching the building.

Authorities said Saari had posted videos on **YouTube** showing himself practicing with a handgun at a shooting range. In one video, he pointed the weapon toward the camera and delivered a threatening statement. The account and videos were removed after the shooting.

Police had questioned Saari one day before the attack after receiving information about the online material. An officer decided there were not sufficient grounds to revoke his temporary firearms permit or seize his weapon, a decision that immediately prompted scrutiny of Finland’s gun laws and police procedures.

Prime Minister **Matti Vanhanen** called the shooting a “tragic day” for Finland and announced a national day of mourning, with flags ordered to fly at half-staff. President **Tarja Halonen** expressed condolences to the victims’ families, while Interior Minister **Anne Holmlund** said authorities would investigate both the attack and the earlier police contact with Saari.

The massacre came less than a year after an 18-year-old gunman killed eight people and himself at Jokela High School in southern Finland, intensifying national debate over firearm access, online threats and school security.

counterfactuals.output:
# Kauhajoki college shooting left 11 dead after online threats and missed warning signs

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland —** A gunman killed 10 people at a college campus in the western Finnish town of Kauhajoki on Sept. 23, 2008, before fatally shooting himself, in an attack that exposed serious failures in how authorities assessed online threats and firearms risks.

The attacker, 22-year-old hospitality-management student Matti Juhani Saari, entered the Kauhajoki campus of the Seinäjoki University of Applied Sciences during the morning, carrying a legally purchased handgun and incendiary materials. He opened fire in a classroom where students were taking an examination.

Nine students and one staff member were killed. Saari also started fires inside the building, filling parts of it with smoke and complicating rescue efforts. Several people escaped through doors and windows, while others hid as the shooting continued.

Emergency calls brought police, firefighters and medical crews to the campus. Armed officers surrounded the building, evacuated survivors and began searching the smoke-filled premises. The fires and uncertainty about the gunman’s location slowed their advance. Saari was eventually found alive with a self-inflicted gunshot wound. He was taken to hospital but died later that day, bringing the total death toll, including the attacker, to 11.

## Police had questioned the gunman the previous day

The attack drew particular scrutiny because Saari had come to police attention before the shooting.

In the days beforehand, he had posted internet videos and photographs showing himself firing a handgun at a shooting range. Some of the material included threatening or aggressive language. The clips resembled online material posted before the 2007 Jokela school shooting, in which another Finnish student killed eight people and himself.

Police received information about Saari’s videos and identified him. An officer interviewed him on Sept. 22, one day before the attack, to assess whether his firearm should be confiscated. Saari had obtained a temporary permit for the small-caliber semiautomatic pistol only weeks earlier.

The officer decided there were not sufficient grounds to seize the weapon or revoke the permit. Saari was allowed to keep the handgun, which he used in the massacre the following morning.

Investigations later found that authorities possessed several pieces of concerning information but failed to combine them into an accurate assessment of the danger. Saari’s firearm videos, violent presentation, access to a recently licensed weapon and reported communications about school shootings formed a pattern that, in retrospect, indicated a potentially serious threat.

A subsequent official inquiry concluded that the police decision-making had been inadequate. The licensing and threat-assessment process was criticized, although legal proceedings did not establish that confiscating the weapon would necessarily have prevented the killings.

## A planned attack

Investigators determined that the shooting was not spontaneous. Saari had prepared for it, brought materials to ignite fires and left behind media intended to publicize his actions. He also expressed admiration for earlier mass killers, including the perpetrator of the Jokela attack.

Authorities examined whether Saari had acted with anyone else but concluded that he carried out the assault alone. His precise motive was never fully established, though investigators described a combination of fascination with mass violence, hostility toward other people and personal psychological difficulties.

The fires badly damaged the building and hindered the identification and recovery of victims. Police and rescue officials later reviewed how emergency services entered the campus, communicated during the attack and managed a scene involving both an active shooter and multiple fires.

## National debate over gun laws and prevention

The Kauhajoki massacre came less than a year after Jokela and forced Finland to confront the recurrence of school shootings in a country with relatively high civilian firearm ownership.

The government tightened handgun licensing rules and increased scrutiny of applicants, particularly younger people seeking pistols. The attack also led to broader monitoring of online threats, changes in information-sharing among police and health authorities, and efforts to improve threat-assessment procedures in schools.

Officials emphasized, however, that internet posts must be evaluated in context and that effective prevention depends on authorities connecting online behavior, access to weapons, personal history and reports from people around a potential attacker.

Kauhajoki remains one of the deadliest peacetime shootings in Finnish history. Its most enduring lesson was the stark warning that the attacker had not been entirely unknown to authorities: police had seen his material, interviewed him and considered taking away his gun — but left him armed less than 24 hours before the killings.

counterfactuals.output:
On **23 September 2008**, a gunman attacked the hospitality department of the **Seinäjoki University of Applied Sciences in Kauhajoki**, western Finland.

- **Attacker:** **Matti Juhani Saari**, a 22-year-old culinary/hospitality student at the school, entered during an examination wearing dark clothing and carrying a legally obtained **.22-calibre Walther P22 pistol**. He opened fire in a classroom, pursued some victims, and set several fires using flammable liquid. He then shot himself in the head and died later in hospital.
- **Victims:** Saari killed **10 people—nine students and one teacher**. Most were members of his class; eight of the student victims were women and one was a man. At least one other person suffered a gunshot wound, and others were treated for injuries or smoke exposure.
- **Online videos:** Before the attack, Saari posted shooting-range videos and photographs online, including on YouTube under the name **“Wumpscut86.”** Some showed him firing the pistol, pointing it toward the camera, and making threatening statements such as **“You will die next.”** The material was removed after the shooting.
- **Gun licence and police contact:** Saari had received a temporary licence for the handgun only weeks earlier. Police learned of his online videos before the massacre and questioned him on **22 September**, the day before the attack. The interviewing officer decided there were insufficient legal grounds to confiscate the weapon or revoke the permit, so Saari retained it. That decision prompted intense criticism and later legal and administrative scrutiny.
- **Parallels to Jokela:** The attack closely resembled the **Jokela school shooting of 7 November 2007**, in which 18-year-old **Pekka-Eric Auvinen** killed eight people and himself. Both attackers were young Finnish students who used legally licensed .22-calibre handguns, advertised themselves through ominous internet videos and images, attacked educational institutions, and died by suicide. Saari appeared to imitate aspects of Auvinen’s online presentation, and investigators examined evidence that the two had moved in overlapping online circles, although no firm proof of a coordinated relationship emerged.

The Kauhajoki massacre led Finland to tighten firearms rules, particularly for young handgun applicants, and intensified debate about how police should respond to online threats.

counterfactuals.output:
**Gunman kills 10 at Finnish college, then shoots himself**

**KAUHAJOKI, Finland, Sept. 23, 2008 (Wire Services)** — A masked gunman opened fire at a vocational college in western Finland on Tuesday, killing 10 people before shooting himself, police said, in the country’s second school massacre in less than a year.

Police identified the attacker as 22-year-old student Matti Juhani Saari. He died later at a hospital in Tampere from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Witnesses said the gunman, dressed in black and carrying a large bag, entered the Kauhajoki School of Hospitality shortly before 11 a.m. and began firing in a classroom where students were taking an examination.

“I heard several dozen rounds of shots,” school caretaker Jukka Forsberg told Reuters. “In other words, it was an automatic pistol.” Forsberg said the attacker fired at him but missed.

Smoke poured from the building after fires were set inside, complicating the police operation and the recovery of victims. Finnish broadcaster YLE reported that some bodies had been badly burned.

Police said nine students and one teacher were killed. Several other people were injured.

“The gunman had a 0.22-calibre handgun, and he had a licence for it,” police official Jari Neulaniemi told reporters. Investigators said officers had questioned Saari only a day earlier after discovering Internet videos in which he was shown firing a pistol, but they had not found sufficient grounds to confiscate the weapon.

Finnish media, including the newspaper *Helsingin Sanomat* and broadcaster MTV3, said clips posted under Saari’s name showed a young man at a shooting range pointing a handgun toward the camera. In one video he says, “You will die next.”

President Tarja Halonen described the killings as a shocking continuation of the November 2007 massacre at Jokela High School, where an 18-year-old gunman killed eight people and himself.

“The day and the events are a tragic continuation of what happened in Jokela less than a year ago,” Halonen said in a televised statement, offering condolences to the victims’ families and the Kauhajoki community.

Prime Minister Matti Vanhanen declared Wednesday a national day of mourning and ordered flags lowered to half-staff.

The shooting renewed debate over Finland’s gun laws. The country has one of Europe’s highest rates of private firearm ownership, largely because of strong hunting and target-shooting traditions. Government officials said proposed restrictions on handgun permits would be reviewed urgently.
